                   MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                      ADVANTAGE CAPITAL RENEWABLES, LLC

         Pursuant to Rules 212 and 2131 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, Advantage Capital Renewables, LLC

(“Advantage Renewables” or “Complainant”) hereby submits this Motion for Leave to Answer

(“Motion”) and Answer (“Answer”) to the answer filed by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”)

on September 8, 20262 in response to the Complaint filed by Advantage Renewables on August

25, 20263 in the above-captioned proceeding.4

 I.      MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

        The Commission’s rules do not, as a matter of right, allow for an answer to a protest or

answer.5 However, the Commission will permit such answers for good cause shown.6 Good cause

exists when the response will assist the Commission in its decision-making process, such as by

helping to explain the relevant issues or otherwise facilitating the development of the record.7

        Good cause exists here to permit Advantage Renewables to file this Answer. The PJM

Answer contains material mischaracterizations and omissions that, if left uncorrected, could

mislead the Commission. This Answer will assist the Commission in its decision-making by

clarifying the record, correcting misstatements in PJM’s Answer, and presenting additional

evidence from the growing record of Cycle 01 complaints filed since Advantage Renewables’

Complaint.

II.     ANSWER

        A.       Advantage Renewables Has Met Its Burden Under Federal Power Act
                 (“FPA”) Section 206, and PJM’s Answer Fails to Rebut the Complaint’s
                 Showing

        As a threshold matter, the Commission should recognize that Advantage Renewables has

met its prima facie burden under FPA Section 206.8 Under FPA Section 206, a complainant must

show that a rate or practice is unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential.9 A

complainant satisfies that burden by “clearly identify[ing] the action or inaction which is alleged

to violate applicable statutory standards or regulatory requirements” and “explain[ing] how the

that showing is made, “the burden of going forward shifts to the opposing party; although the

ultimate burden of proof remains with the proponent.”11 Advantage Renewables’ Complaint

clearly identified PJM’s failures and explained how they violate the Tariff and the FPA.12 Having

established a prima facie case, the burden shifted to PJM. PJM’s Answer does not rebut the

Complaint’s showing.

        Indeed, the Complaint identified multiple, independent violations of the Tariff and the

FPA,13 including that: PJM failed to communicate stability-related deficiencies during the Tariff-

defined notice-and-cure period and then withdrew the Freshwater Dune Project based on those

undisclosed deficiencies;14 PJM enforced unfiled Dynamic Model Development Guidelines

(“DMDG”) requirements as queue-eligibility conditions without Commission approval;15 and PJM

treated similarly situated Cycle 01 projects differently without justification.16 Each of these

showings independently satisfies Advantage Renewables’ prima facie burden under FPA Section

206, and PJM’s Answer does not adequately rebut that showing. Notably, PJM offers no clear

evidence that it communicated the stability deficiencies during the cure period, no authority for

enforcing unfiled requirements as valid grounds to withdraw a project from its interconnection

queue, and no justification for the disparate treatment documented in the record in this

proceeding.17 Moreover, PJM’s response—that the comments were “available” in NextGen—does

not rebut the Complaint’s showing that PJM failed to “inform” Advantage Renewables of

        B.       PJM’s Answer Further Demonstrates that PJM Violated Its Own Tariff
                 Procedures

                i.        Advantage Renewables Responded to All Deficiencies Communicated to It
                          During the Cure Period

        PJM asserts that it “did not deviate from its Application Review Phase procedures as

prescribed in the Tariff” and that the withdrawal “was based on the Project Developer’s failure to

correct identified deficiencies set forth in PJM's Deficiency Notice.”20 PJM further claims that the

eight operative stability comments “were all contained within one data field in NextGen” and were

“available for the Complainant’s review during the cure period,” placing the “onus” on Advantage

Renewables to find and address them. But PJM’s own communications and the record in this

proceeding tell a different story.21 Notably, PJM’s Withdrawal Notice referenced “round 1” and

“round 2,” language that indicates that PJM engaged in a second review of Advantage Renewables’

cure submission.22 However, PJM now characterizes the review differently, stating in the PJM

Answer that there was no second round review and that it merely “reviewed the Deficiency

Responses and determined that the deficiency comments were not resolved.”23 Regardless of how

PJM characterizes its process, the critical point is that Section 403(B) permits PJM to review the

cure package and to validate or reject the Application, but it does not permit PJM to reject an

 Application based on deficiencies PJM failed to adequately communicate during the notice-and-

cure period.

        Section 403(B)(1)(a)-(c) prescribes a closed, three-step sequence with a binary outcome:

PJM must identify deficiencies, the Applicant has ten Business Days to respond, and PJM must

then review the response and validate or reject the Application.24 As indicated, PJM now contends

that the comments that served as a basis to remove the Freshwater Dune Project were all “identified

in the June 2, 2026 deficiency notice” and that it merely “reviewed the Deficiency Responses and

determined that the deficiency comments were not resolved.”25 PJM’s admission that the second

round comments were merely “advisory” and “intended to provide guidance in the event

Complainant chooses to apply its Project in a future cycle”26 means that PJM admits that the second

round comments cannot serve as a valid basis for withdrawing the Freshwater Dune Project.

Accordingly, whether the withdrawal of the Freshwater Dune Project was justified under the Tariff

must stand or fall on whether Advantage Renewables addressed the deficiencies that PJM

communicated during the cure period.

        The record unequivocally demonstrates that Advantage Renewables’ June 16 submission

addressed every deficiency PJM actually communicated to it during the cure period, including the

short-circuit and load-flow comments to which PJM directed it.27 Indeed, with respect to the non-

stability deficiencies (i.e., the deficiencies that were actually communicated to Advantage

Renewables pursuant to the Tariff and during the cure period), PJM later confirmed that load-flow

data was “acceptable and approved” on June 16, 2026, and that “Site Control [was] approved” on

communicated to Advantage Renewables, and PJM does not contend otherwise.

                ii.       PJM Did Not Inform Advantage Renewables of Any Remaining Alleged
                          Deficiencies As Required by the Tariff

deficiencies to Advantage Renewables,35 and PJM stated that Advantage Renewables’ failure to

respond to these stability-related deficiencies were part of the justification for withdrawing the

Freshwater Dune Project.36            However, PJM had an affirmative obligation under Section

 403(B)(1)(a) to “inform Applicant of Application deficiencies.”37 The obligation to “inform”

requires clear and specific notice identifying the particular deficiencies at issue; it is not satisfied

by the mere existence of comments in a portal database — some of which the Applicant was never

directed to review.38

         PJM’s failure to identify the alleged stability-related deficiencies,39 particularly when

directly asked by Advantage Renewables, constituted a failure by PJM to provide adequate notice

and “inform” an Applicant of alleged deficiencies as required by the Tariff.40                             Given that

Advantage Renewables was never informed of the stability-related deficiencies, Advantage

Renewables’ alleged failure to address them cannot serve as a valid basis for withdrawing the

Freshwater Dune Project. Simply put, PJM’s Tariff obligation is not satisfied by the alleged, mere

existence of comments somewhere in a portal database that an Applicant was never directed to

review—it requires active, targeted communication identifying the specific deficiencies, and PJM

failed to provide it. PJM cannot satisfy that obligation by asserting that comments were “available”

merely because they were allegedly timestamped in NextGen.

Indeed, Oklo Inc. (“Oklo”) recently described PJM’s practice of “quietly” placing reviewer

and PJM staff confirmed receipt.46 Indeed, this very exchange underscores the inadequacy of

        These events beg the question of why the stability comments, which were allegedly

available in NextGen, were not communicated to Advantage Renewables when Ms. Neha directly

asked PJM to identify any remaining deficiencies before the deadline? Based on the record in this

proceeding, the most likely explanation is that these comments were not in fact available in

NextGen when it counted. Regardless, whether the stability comments were in fact in the NextGen

portal but hidden, did not exist, were not communicated to Ms. Neha as a result of human error,

or were unavailable due to some other explanation, it does not change the fact that PJM failed to

comply with its affirmative Tariff obligation to “inform [Advantage Renewables] of Application

deficiencies,” and therefore, Advantage Renewables’ failure to respond to the stability-related

deficiencies cannot serve as a valid ground to remove the Freshwater Dune Project because the

stability-related deficiencies were never communicated to Advantage Renewables in the time and

manner prescribed by the Tariff.

       Alternatively, even if the Commission finds that stability-related deficiencies existed, they

are readily curable and do not warrant removal of the Freshwater Dune Project from Cycle 01.

Advantage Renewables can promptly provide any remaining files or clarifications. The remaining

items identified in PJM’s Withdrawal Notice are documentation-level reconciliations and technical

file-format issues—matters that can be resolved through targeted data submissions and do not

reflect any fundamental flaw in the project’s engineering design or feasibility. Indeed, Advantage

Renewables has already undertaken preparatory work to address the remaining items in the

Withdrawal Notice and is prepared to provide updated submissions to PJM within three business

days if given the opportunity. The remaining items—documentation-level reconciliations such as

updated file formats, model configuration adjustments, and supplemental DMDG package

materials—do not require fundamental re-engineering and can be resolved through targeted data



                                                10
 submissions. Advantage Renewables requested reinstatement or, alternatively, the opportunity to

cure precisely because the alleged deficiencies are easily remediable.53 PJM, however, is using a

portal or review-process failure to justify withdrawal of the Freshwater Dune Project even though

a short additional cure period would resolve the issue. In the context of ordering remedial relief

in an FPA Section 206 proceeding, this is well within the Commission’s authority to direct.54

         Further, as discussed in detail in Section E below, the Freshwater Dune Project is a 100

MW battery project in a Cycle of more than 200 GW, the alleged deficiencies are technical and

readily addressable, and reinstatement would not materially disrupt Cycle 01. Advantage

Renewables does not seek an exemption from the Tariff, a waiver of any requirement, or

preferential treatment relative to other Cycle 01 participants. It seeks the opposite: performance

under the Tariff as written.

         C.       PJM’s Arguments Do Not Demonstrate that the DMDG May Be Omitted from
                  the Tariff Under the Rule of Reason and Filed Rate Doctrine

         PJM argues that “the DMDG requirements should not be filed in the Tariff, as the

Application requirements are clear,” and that the Commission’s rule of reason permits PJM to

relegate the DMDG to its manuals and guidelines.55 PJM further contends that “even significant

and specifiable practices need not be in a tariff when they are clearly implied by the tariff’s express

terms” and that Section 403(A) “does more than imply, but explicitly requires Project Developers

to submit a Completed Application that includes all information required under the Tariff, as

operational flexibility, to keep up with ever changing technological advancements.”57 Each of

these contentions fails.

        As a threshold matter, PJM’s attempt to argue that the Freshwater Dune Project was

removed due to “deficiencies” rather than adherence to the “DMDG requirements” is a misleading

and frivolous argument.58 PJM acknowledges that the allegedly unresolved deficiency comments

all “related to the dynamic model.”59 PJM’s own Exhibit 3 to its answer maps each comment to

specific DMDG deliverables—including Dynamic Model Reports, PSSE files, PQ curves, DLL

files, and model configurations—and the Withdrawal Notice states that the project “[f]ailed to

meet Stability requirements” and references “the DMDG package.”60 Accordingly, PJM withdrew

the Freshwater Dune Project because it allegedly did not satisfy requirements set forth in the

unfiled DMDG. PJM’s attempt at obfuscation on this point does not change the analysis of

whether the DMDG requirements should have been filed in the Tariff under the rule of reason or

the filed rate doctrine, which would be required in order for them to serve as a valid basis to remove

the Freshwater Dune Project from the interconnection queue.

        Contrary to PJM’s assertions, the DMDG requirements go well beyond “implementation

details” and materially expand what PJM treats as a complete Application. PJM is enforcing a

new, material category of stability-related information that has no anchor in the Tariff. The D.C.

Circuit’s decision in Hecate Energy Greene County 3 LLC v. FERC (“Hecate”) holds that practices

need not be filed only when “clearly implied by the tariff’s express terms”—a standard PJM cannot

 satisfy because Section 403(A)(1) – which specifies the criteria necessary to have a completed

Application- says nothing about PSSE versions, dynamic model files, or DMDG deliverables.61

The DMDG requirements include specific software, file, reporting, and configuration obligations

that are entirely absent from Section 403(A)(1).62

        PJM asserts that Section 403(A) “does more than imply, but explicitly requires Project

Developers to submit a Completed Application that includes all information required under the

Tariff, as detailed further in the Application and PJM’s Manuals.”63 But Section 403(A)(1)

contains no “stability requirements” category for a complete Application. Indeed, Section

403(A)(1) enumerates several specific categories of information required for a complete

Application—including the requirements to “[p]rovide a detailed description of the equipment

configuration and electrical design specifications for the Generating Facility,” “[s]pecify the fuel

type,” and “[s]pecify the proposed date that the project . . . will be in service”—but none of these

required categories references PSSE versions, dynamic model files, DMDG deliverables, or

stability-related requirements.64 PJM cannot hide entire categories of material information that it

deems necessary to have a completed Application in unfiled guidelines that are not even part of

PJM’s manuals.

        By requiring “stability requirements” submitted in accordance with the DMDG guidelines

in order to have a completed Application, PJM is creating a new substantive obligation for

Applicants, not merely documenting the Tariff’s implementation details. PJM invokes Energy

 Storage Ass’n as an alleged favorable authority for its position.65 But PJM ignores the holding in

that decision that matters: the Commission in Energy Storage Ass’n found that PJM’s benefits

factor methodology was “not a mere implementation detail” precisely because it “significantly

impacts” resource participation. The DMDG requirements at issue here are even more

consequential—they determined whether the Freshwater Dune Project could remain in the queue

at all. PJM illogically cites Energy Storage Ass’n for its favorable dicta while ignoring the

decision’s holding that outcome-determinative requirements such as the DMDG requirements

must be filed in order to be enforced. Accordingly, Energy Storage Ass’n undercuts, rather than

supports, PJM’s position.

        PJM also argues that the DMDG “should not be filed in the Tariff, since PJM must retain

operational flexibility, to keep up with ever changing technological advancements.”66 That

argument, if accepted, would swallow whole the requirement to have any filed rate at all. If PJM’s

position were to be accepted, any RTO could adopt material, outcome-determinative

requirements—readily susceptible of specification and not anchored in a tariff’s express terms—

and then invoke “operational flexibility” to excuse itself from filing them. The result would be that

the rule of reason and the filed rate doctrine would impose no meaningful constraint on an RTO’s

conduct, because every unfiled requirement could be excused as an exercise of “operational

flexibility.” That is precisely the kind of absurd result that Commission precedent forbids.67

        The FPA provides PJM a clear path to update its requirements as technology evolves: it

can file tariff amendments under FPA Section 205 and obtain prospective Commission approval.

In fact, under Hecate, all PJM needs to do is “anchor” the stability requirement category in the

        PJM also asserts that Advantage Renewables has not “identified any DMDG requirements

that contradict the Tariff.”70 That argument misses the point. The rule of reason does not ask

whether unfiled requirements contradict the Tariff; it asks whether they “significantly affect rates,

terms, and conditions of service,” are “readily susceptible of specification,” and are “not generally

understood in a contractual agreement.”71 Requirements need not contradict a tariff provision to

reside in manuals. For example, in ISO New England Inc., the Commission set aside a prior order

and required ISO-NE to file tariff revisions specifying submetering requirements for distributed

energy resource aggregations, because failure to satisfy those requirements could prevent

Q. WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR AFFIDAVIT?
A. This affidavit supports the Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer filed by Advantage
Renewables in the above-captioned proceeding. Specifically, I am providing testimony regarding
my direct experience with PJM’s NextGen portal during the deficiency cure period for the
Freshwater Dune Project (Queue No. C01-1742), including PJM’s failure to identify stability-
 related deficiency comments when I sought direct guidance from PJM by email, having
encountered unexpected difficulty submitting the project in the NextGen portal.
Q. PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR EXPERIENCE USING PJM’S NEXTGEN PORTAL
A. I submitted two projects myself via the NextGen portal. I have used the NextGen portal
regularly during my tenure at Advantage Renewables, both to submit new applications and to track
and monitor the status of projects. I have been using NextGen since PJM began the rollout of
NextGen in March of 2025, at which time I had already been a part of Advantage Renewables’
engineering team for approximately two years.
Q. PLEASE DESCRIBE HOW THE SUBMISSION PROCESS WORKS ON NEXTGEN
A. The NextGen portal allows you to select a particular project and see past and future submissions
due to PJM and PJM’s responses. When submitting information to PJM, there are often multiple
tabs of requested information, and you must enter information in each box that requests a response
in order for the portal to accept the submission. If you miss entering any requested information,
you receive an error message and must provide the missing information before submitting.
Q. PLEASE DESCRIBE THE DEFICIENCY CURE SUBMISSION ON NEXTGEN
A. On June 15, 2026, a PJM representative emailed a reminder that the deficiency cure
submission was due the next day. By June 16, 2026, Advantage Renewables had prepared its
cure materials, which addressed each of the deficiencies PJM had identified in its June 2, 2026
Deficiency Notice, including: corrected attachment-line zero-sequence impedance values; a
revised single-line diagram; updated dynamic files, including an updated dynamic model
reflecting the REGCA low-voltage parameter value PJM had identified, together with an updated
Dynamic Model Development Guidelines (“DMDG”) package; updated total line miles; supplied
missing R0 and X0 transformer values; an updated Officer Certification and site control
evidence; and responses to the short-circuit and load-flow comments at the locations in NextGen
to which PJM directed us.

When I attempted to submit the cure materials through the NextGen portal, I received an error
message stating that “all deficiencies must be commented on or submitted before submitting.” I
understood this error to mean that the portal operated as a completeness check and would not
permit a response to be submitted while any identified deficiency remained unaddressed. I could
not locate the outstanding uncommented fields the portal was referring to.

I wrote to PJM immediately on the same day, stating: “I am trying to submit but I am getting [an]
error from NextGen saying that all deficiencies must be commented on or submitted before
submitting. Can you please help with finding what the issue is?”

A few hours later, a PJM representative responded with a screenshot identifying only two fields
under the Main Transformer section of the Transformer Information tab that had not been
commented on. The PJM representative did not identify any stability comment. The
representative did not refer me to the Dynamic File(s) section, to the stability reviewer’s
comment, or to any other outstanding item.




                                                2
 I commented on those two Main Transformer fields, and the portal then permitted the submission
to proceed. I requested confirmation that the submission was received, and a PJM representative
responded: “Thank you Farah, we have received your submission.”
Q. DID PJM CONFIRM THAT ANY OF THE NON-STABILITY DEFICIENCIES
WERE SATISFACTORILY ADDRESSED?
A. Yes. On June 16, 2026, a PJM comment in NextGen confirmed that “Load flow data is
acceptable and approved.” On July 7, 2026, a PJM comment confirmed that “Site Control
approved.” PJM has never disputed these determinations. These confirmations reinforced my
understanding that the cure submission had been satisfactorily received and that PJM had
reviewed and accepted the responses to the deficiencies it had communicated.
Q. HOW DID PJM’S JUNE 2, 2026 DEFICIENCY NOTICE ADDRESS STABILITY?
A. The Deficiency Notice included an Additional Comment stating, in its entirety: “Stability data
is deficient.” Unlike the short-circuit reviewer, who wrote “Short Circuit data is deficient. Please
see comments in NextGen and address deficiencies during cure period,” and the load-flow
reviewer, who wrote “Load flow data is deficient. Please see comments in POI section,” the
stability comment identified no section, no field, and no location, and did not direct me to review
anything specific. In response to this general statement, I submitted an updated dynamic model,
including the REGCA low-voltage parameter value PJM had identified, together with an updated
DMDG package.
Q. PLEASE DESCRIBE THE SUBSEQUENT CORRESPONDENCE WITH PJM
A. On August 3, 2026, Advantage Renewables was notified by PJM that our project, the
Freshwater Dune Project, had been withdrawn from PJM’s Cycle 01 interconnection queue. The
Withdrawal Notice stated that the project “[f]ailed to meet Stability requirements” and that the
DMDG package “was provided but it is still missing multiple files and has several deficiencies.”
The Withdrawal Notice listed fourteen deficiencies, including requirements that PJM had not
identified, or had materially reformulated, during the cure period.
Q. WERE ALL OF THE DEFICIENCIES LISTED IN THE WITHDRAWAL NOTICE
IDENTIFIED DURING THE CURE PERIOD?
A. No. The stability-related deficiencies cited in the Withdrawal Notice were never
communicated to me or to Advantage Renewables during the cure period. When I asked PJM
directly, in writing and before the deadline, to identify what remained outstanding on the
Application, PJM reviewed the Application and identified only two Transformer Information
fields. Had PJM identified the stability comments in that same response, I would have addressed
them in the same submission, as I did the two fields PJM identified.
Q. DID YOU CHECK THE NEXTGEN PORTAL DURING THE CURE PERIOD?
A. Yes. I regularly reviewed deficiency comments as they were published on the NextGen portal
throughout the cure period. I checked the portal multiple times to monitor the status of our
submission and to review any feedback from PJM reviewers.

 Q. IN THE NEXTGEN PORTAL, WERE ANY COMMENTS PUBLISHED ON MAY 7
OR 8 REGARDING THE STABILITY-RELATED DEFICIENCIES VISIBLE?
A. The stability-related comments that PJM claims were timestamped May 7–8, 2026 were not
visible to me on the NextGen portal when I reviewed it during the cure period. I cannot explain
why those comments appear timestamped in the system today but were not visible to me at the
time. Whatever the explanation—whether a portal display error, a delayed posting, or some other
system issue—I did not see those comments, and they were not flagged by the portal as requiring
a response before my submission could be completed.
Moreover, when I specifically asked PJM to help me identify what remained outstanding on the
Application, PJM reviewed the Application and responded by identifying only two fields under
the Transformer Information tab—PJM did not identify any stability comment, did not refer me
to the Dynamic File(s) section, and did not mention any other outstanding item. If those stability-
related comments had existed and been visible at that time, I would have expected PJM to
identify them in response to my direct request for help.
Q. DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR AFFIDAVIT?
A. Yes.
